Ava — looping my suggested alternative (high level first, legal draft to follow):

Operational compromise (Option A):
1) Trigger: 30% decline vs. 90-day rolling baseline, measured at calendar quarter granularity; triggers require two consecutive quarters below threshold to avoid short blips.
2) Remediation window: upon trigger, parties will engage a 45-day reconciliation: temporary smoothing credit applied to next invoice while parties agree the true-up mechanics.
3) Caps: any reopener increase limited to 12% per quarter with a 20% annual ceiling.
4) True-ups: downward true-ups if consumption recovers within 12 months will be netted against future invoices; no retroactive refunds after 12 months.

Rationale: 90-day baseline + two-quarter confirmation protects us from transient churn and seasonal anomalies. The cap numbers reduce our downside while giving Orion a measurable path.

I put examples in the shared spreadsheet: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/drive-example (we should replace with internal link). Marissa — see the 'P&L_Scenarios' tab for modeled outcomes (best/expected/worst).

If legal (Neha) prefers, we can compress to once-per-year reopener but that weakens Orion's ask — may not get signed.

Team — legal redlines attached and summarized below (see redline_summary.txt). I tried to preserve commercial intent while removing language that creates ambiguous "reopener" mechanics. Key legal positions: 

1) Trigger definition: replace "60-day window" language with a clear metric: "Monthly billable tokens averaged over a rolling 90-day period compared to the average of the prior two completed quarters; a reopener will be available if the drop is >=30% and persists for two consecutive quarters."

2) Reopener frequency: limit to once in any 12-month period unless both parties agree in writing.

3) Cap and smoothing: accept a phase-in for increases but cap the aggregate increase resulting from a reopener at 15% in any 12-month period; however, require that the cap not apply to pricing changes tied to material cost pass-throughs (we can list examples).

4) Remedies and credits: downward reconciliations may be credited to future invoices within 12 months; no retroactive cash refunds.

I'm attaching redline_summary.txt with line-by-line notes and a draft clause (see section 4) that Karthik can review for operational feasibility. If we want to be more aggressive commercially, I can draft a 'sales-friendly' variant that allows a 20% trigger but only annual review.

Dana / Orion legal — thanks for the redlines and for the constructive conversation. We've reviewed internally and can align on a compromise approach to present back to you. Summary of Redwood's consolidated position: 

1) Trigger: 30% decline from the baseline measured over a rolling 90-day period, confirmed by two consecutive quarters below the baseline. This balances Orion's concern about step-changes with Redwood's need to avoid transient blips.

2) Frequency: reopener may be invoked no more than once in any 12-month period, absent written agreement otherwise.

3) Cap & smoothing: Redwood will accept phased implementation of any reopener-driven price change over two quarters, with an aggregate cap of 15% in any 12-month period. We retain carveouts for extraordinary cost pass-throughs (example: new GPU tax or third-party licensing jump).

4) True-ups: downward reconciliations will be credited to future invoices for up to 12 months; no cash refunds beyond that window.

Next steps:
